node.label: Settler colonialism
node.date_label: Earlier settler-society studies 1983–95 · Wolfe 1999 · coverage through 2000; selected later readings: Wolfe 2006, Veracini 2010, journal 2011, critiques 2013–20; field chronology unresolved

date_span.basis: Selected publication milestones only. 1983 and 1995 are earlier settler-society witnesses, not the field's origin; Wolfe 1999 is the only selected milestone inside 1920–2000. Naming and consolidation fall after 2000; neither endpoint bounds the field.

node.description: Historical inquiry into colonial formations in which newcomers came to stay, acquired land and claimed sovereignty over Indigenous territories. Patrick Wolfe's account of settler colonialism as a structure rather than an event treats invasion as a continuing relation rather than a completed frontier past. Lorenzo Veracini's work and the journal Settler Colonial Studies (2011) distinguished settler colonial from colonial phenomena. Comparative studies of settler capitalism and settler societies, and decolonization-era uses of the term, came earlier. In Canadian historical writing the framework meets an older historiography of dispossession, reserves, gender and the state in the West and British Columbia. It also meets Indigenous political theory of recognition, sovereignty and resurgence. Its uses extend to labour, science, memory and settler identity. The field is contested from several directions. Indigenous scholars ask whether it recentres settlers and displaces Indigenous studies and Indigenous-authored histories. Historians question its structural inevitability and its fit across regions and periods, proposing other modes such as commercial penetration and extractivism. Black studies scholars question how it places slavery. Settler colonialism overlaps with Indigenous history, postcolonial critique and historical geography without being equivalent to any of them.
node.scope_note: A selective research field whose theoretical consolidation came mostly after 2000; the entry covers its roots through 2000 and cites selected later works as readings. Settler-colonial theory, Indigenous political thought, Canadian histories of dispossession and comparative imperial history have different genealogies. Roster inclusion is not adoption of the paradigm: Carter, Perry, Harris and Daschuk wrote earlier or beside it. No single founder, origin or Canadian consensus is asserted. Critics appear as critics. Francophone uptake in the PhD corpus is near zero.
node.representative_figures_and_works: Earlier: Denoon, Settler Capitalism (1983); Stasiulis and Yuval-Davis, eds., Unsettling Settler Societies (1995). Wolfe, Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology (1999) and “Settler Colonialism and the Elimination of the Native” (2006); Elkins and Pedersen, eds. (2005); Veracini, Settler Colonialism (2010) and Settler Colonial Studies (2011). Read with Coulthard (2014), A. Simpson (2014), L. B. Simpson (2011, 2017), Byrd (2011) and Tuck and Yang (2012). Canadian historiography: Carter (1990, 2008), Harris (2002, 2004, 2020), Perry (2001), Regan (2010), Daschuk (2013), Battell Lowman and Barker (2015), Burrill (2019). Critiques: Macoun and Strakosch (2013), Rowse (2014), Kauanui (2016), Greer (2019), Shoemaker (2019), Konishi (2019), Garba and Sorentino (2020).

strands.title: Structure, not event
strands.focus: Wolfe's account treats invasion and elimination as a continuing structure. Kauanui's abstract attests the formulation and its critique; Wolfe's own pages are not checked here.
strands.works: Patrick Wolfe, Settler Colonialism and the Transformation of Anthropology: The Politics and Poetics of an Ethnographic Event (London and New York: Cassell, 1999). Writing Past Colonialism series.; Patrick Wolfe, "Land, Labor, and Difference: Elementary Structures of Race," American Historical Review 106, no. 3 (2001): 866–905.; Patrick Wolfe, "Settler Colonialism and the Elimination of the Native," Journal of Genocide Research 8, no. 4 (2006): 387–409.; J. Kēhaulani Kauanui, "'A Structure, Not an Event': Settler Colonialism and Enduring Indigeneity," Lateral 5, no. 1 (2016).

strands.title: Settler colonial theory and field formation
strands.focus: Veracini disentangles settler colonial from colonial phenomena and introduces a dedicated journal (2011); a 2013 essay traces the concept's earlier career. Field-making, not a claim of single origin.
strands.works: Lorenzo Veracini, "Settler Collective, Founding Violence and Disavowal: The Settler Colonial Situation," Journal of Intercultural Studies 29, no. 4 (2008): 363–379.; Lorenzo Veracini, Settler Colonialism: A Theoretical Overview (Basingstoke: Palgrave Macmillan, 2010).; Lorenzo Veracini, "Introducing: Settler Colonial Studies," Settler Colonial Studies 1, no. 1 (2011): 1–12.; Lorenzo Veracini, "'Settler Colonialism': Career of a Concept," Journal of Imperial and Commonwealth History 41, no. 2 (2013): 313–333.; Edward Cavanagh and Lorenzo Veracini, eds., The Routledge Handbook of the History of Settler Colonialism (London: Routledge, 2017).

strands.title: Settler capitalism and settler societies in comparison
strands.focus: Comparative settler economies (1983) and gender, race, ethnicity and class in settler societies (1995) are earlier comparative scholarship, before the field's theoretical consolidation; Veracini's history of the concept records decolonization-era usage of the term itself.
strands.works: Donald Denoon, Settler Capitalism: The Dynamics of Dependent Development in the Southern Hemisphere (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1983).; Daiva Stasiulis and Nira Yuval-Davis, eds., Unsettling Settler Societies: Articulations of Gender, Race, Ethnicity and Class (London: SAGE, 1995).; Lorenzo Veracini, "'Settler Colonialism': Career of a Concept," Journal of Imperial and Commonwealth History 41, no. 2 (2013): 313–333.

strands.title: Comparative and twentieth-century settler colonies
strands.focus: Comparative collections and studies beyond the British settler dominions, including African settler and native political identities.
strands.works: Caroline Elkins and Susan Pedersen, eds., Settler Colonialism in the Twentieth Century: Projects, Practices, Legacies (New York: Routledge, 2005).; Mahmood Mamdani, "Beyond Settler and Native as Political Identities: Overcoming the Political Legacy of Colonialism," Comparative Studies in Society and History 43, no. 4 (2001): 651–664.; Mahmood Mamdani, Neither Settler nor Native: The Making and Unmaking of Permanent Minorities (Cambridge, MA: Harvard University Press, 2020).

strands.title: Indigenous critiques of recognition, sovereignty and resurgence
strands.focus: Indigenous political theory read alongside the paradigm. These works have their own genealogies in Indigenous thought and are not a subset of settler-colonial studies. Open question: these may belong in Indigenous history instead.

strands.title: Dispossession, reserves and colonial geography in Canada
strands.focus: Harris explains reserve-making as geographical dispossession, backed by state power, capital and settlers, and later reflects on the framework's boundaries. Carter's prairie reserve agriculture predates the paradigm.
strands.works: Cole Harris, The Resettlement of British Columbia: Essays on Colonialism and Geographical Change (Vancouver: UBC Press, 1997).; Cole Harris, Making Native Space: Colonialism, Resistance, and Reserves in British Columbia (Vancouver: UBC Press, 2002).; Cole Harris, "How Did Colonialism Dispossess? Comments from an Edge of Empire," Annals of the Association of American Geographers 94, no. 1 (2004): 165–182.; Cole Harris, A Bounded Land: Reflections on Settler Colonialism in Canada (Vancouver: UBC Press, 2020).; Sarah Carter, Lost Harvests: Prairie Indian Reserve Farmers and Government Policy (Montreal and Kingston: McGill-Queen's University Press, 1990).

strands.title: Gender, family and colonial nation-making
strands.focus: Gender, race, marriage and child removal in colonial British Columbia, the Prairie West, the American West and Australia. Metadata level only.
strands.works: Adele Perry, On the Edge of Empire: Gender, Race, and the Making of British Columbia, 1849–1871 (Toronto: University of Toronto Press, 2001).; Sarah Carter, The Importance of Being Monogamous: Marriage and Nation Building in Western Canada to 1915 (Edmonton: University of Alberta Press / Athabasca University Press, 2008).; Margaret D. Jacobs, White Mother to a Dark Race: Settler Colonialism, Maternalism, and the Removal of Indigenous Children in the American West and Australia, 1880–1940 (Lincoln: University of Nebraska Press, 2009).

strands.title: Settler identity, truth telling and reconciliation
strands.focus: Settler self-examination after residential schools and in contemporary Canada; Regan's contents page names the 'peacemaker myth'.
strands.works: Paulette Regan, Unsettling the Settler Within: Indian Residential Schools, Truth Telling, and Reconciliation in Canada (Vancouver: UBC Press, 2010). Razack, ed., Race, Space, and the Law: Unmapping a White Settler Society (Toronto: Between the Lines, 2002).

strands.title: Health, starvation and state policy
strands.focus: Co-citation places Daschuk's Plains history next to Wolfe and Veracini (19 of 58 Wolfe/Veracini-citing PhDs). Its own framing is unchecked, so this is a comparison strand.
strands.works: James Daschuk, Clearing the Plains: Disease, Politics of Starvation, and the Loss of Aboriginal Life (Regina: University of Regina Press, 2013).

strands.title: Labour and the settler order
strands.focus: Integrates settler workers' ongoing appropriation of Indigenous land into Canadian working-class history.
strands.works: Fred Burrill, "The Settler Order Framework: Rethinking Canadian Working-Class History," Labour/Le Travail 83 (2019): 173–197.

strands.title: Critiques: structure, region and period
strands.focus: Structural inevitability (Macoun and Strakosch), a teleology of elimination (Rowse), regional and periodic fit with other modes of colonialism (Greer), universal theory or English heritage (Shoemaker).
strands.works: Alissa Macoun and Elizabeth Strakosch, "The Ethical Demands of Settler Colonial Theory," Settler Colonial Studies 3, nos. 3–4 (2013): 426–443.; Tim Rowse, "Indigenous Heterogeneity," Australian Historical Studies 45, no. 3 (2014): 297–310.; Allan Greer, "Settler Colonialism and Beyond," Journal of the Canadian Historical Association / Revue de la Société historique du Canada 30, no. 1 (2019): 61–86.; Allan Greer, "Settler Colonialism and Empire in Early America," William and Mary Quarterly 76, no. 3 (2019): 383–390.; Nancy Shoemaker, "Settler Colonialism: Universal Theory or English Heritage?" strands.title: Indigenous scholars on settler colonial studies
strands.focus: Whether the field recentres settlers and displaces Indigenous studies and Indigenous-authored histories.
strands.works: Shino Konishi, "First Nations Scholars, Settler Colonial Studies, and Indigenous History," Australian Historical Studies 50, no. 3 (2019): 285–304.; J. Kēhaulani Kauanui, "'A Structure, Not an Event': Settler Colonialism and Enduring Indigeneity," Lateral 5, no. 1 (2016).; Corey Snelgrove, Rita Kaur Dhamoon and Jeff Corntassel, "Unsettling Settler Colonialism: The Discourse and Politics of Settlers, and Solidarity with Indigenous Nations," Decolonization: Indigeneity, Education & Society 3, no. 2 (2014): 1–32.

strands.title: Slavery and Black studies critiques
strands.focus: How settler-colonial and decolonial frameworks place slavery and Black people.
strands.works: Tapji Garba and Sara-Maria Sorentino, "Slavery Is a Metaphor: A Critical Commentary on Eve Tuck and K. Wayne Yang's 'Decolonization Is Not a Metaphor'," Antipode 52, no. 3 (2020): 764–782.; Jared Sexton, "The Vel of Slavery: Tracking the Figure of the Unsovereign," Critical Sociology 42, nos. 4–5 (2016): 583–597.; Tiffany Lethabo King, The Black Shoals: Offshore Formations of Black and Native Studies (Durham: Duke University Press, 2019).

relation_to_periods: The atlas's main period is 1920–2000. Only precursors (1983, 1995) and Wolfe 1999 fall inside it; the name, journal, Canadian uptake and critiques are post-2000. Recommended: an extension entry like digital_history, with period null, kept out of the exact-2000 baseline (1.121). The existing Indigenous strand 'settler_colonial_interlocutor' (Wolfe 1999) can stay as the in-period cross-reference.

proposed_relationships.relationship: Challenges settler national narratives of empty land and peaceful settlement
proposed_relationships.evidence_note: Veracini's history of the concept describes earlier writing that placed pioneering in 'empty' settings and disavowed Indigenous presence. Regan's contents page names 'Deconstructing Canada's Peacemaker Myth'. Targets settler national narratives, not every national history.

Veracini dates a usage, until the late 1970s, naming a diehard hyper-colonialism challenged by anti-colonial insurgencies. Mamdani revisits the first postcolonial generation's political economy (Rodney) to ask how settler and native became political identities. Comparison: no line of descent from liberation politics to the later field is asserted.

Harris explains British Columbia's reserve system as geographical dispossession resting on state power, capital and settlers, rather than primarily on discourse. He later reflects on the boundaries of settler colonialism (postscript title). It keeps the existing spatial–Indigenous comparison edge_777 separate.
